draft.title: Volumes of solids of revolution
card: Rotate the region under a curve y = f(x), from x = a to x = b, once around the x-axis. This makes a solid. Each slice of it is a thin disc with radius y.
A disc has area πy², so the volume is V = π ∫ y² dx, from x = a to x = b. Square y first, then integrate.
For a rotation about the y-axis, swap the roles of x and y: V = π ∫ x² dy, from y = c to y = d. Write x in terms of y first.
Example: y = x from x = 0 to x = 3 gives a cone. V = π ∫ x² dx = π[x³/3] from 0 to 3 = π(9 − 0) = 9π.
draft.remember: Square the radius, multiply by π, then integrate along the axis of rotation.

a.q: The curve y = √x, from x = 0 to x = 4, is rotated about the x-axis. What is the volume of the solid?
a.why: V = π ∫ (√x)² dx = π ∫ x dx = π[x²/2] from 0 to 4 = π × 8 = 8π. Writing π ∫ √x dx gives 16π/3, which is wrong because y was not squared first.
a.clue: Square y before you integrate, and (√x)² is simple.

b.q: The region under y = 2x from x = 1 to x = 2 is rotated about the x-axis. What is the volume of the solid?
b.why: V = π ∫ (2x)² dx = π ∫ 4x² dx = π[4x³/3] from 1 to 2 = π(32/3 − 4/3) = 28π/3. Forgetting to square the 2 gives 14π/3, which is wrong because the radius is 2x, so the 2 is squared too.
b.clue: The radius is 2x, so square the whole of it, including the 2.

check.summary: No problems found. Both answers check out (8π and 28π/3), the cone example is correct (9π), and the distractors reflect realistic errors.

final.title: Volumes of solids of revolution
card: Rotate the region under a curve \(y = f(x)\), from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\), once around the x-axis. This makes a solid. Each slice of it is a thin disc with radius \(y\).
A disc has area \(\pi y^{2}\), so the volume is \(V = \pi \int y^{2} \, dx\), from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\). Square \(y\) first, then integrate.
For a rotation about the y-axis, swap the roles of \(x\) and \(y\): \(V = \pi \int x^{2} \, dy\), from \(y = c\) to \(y = d\). Write \(x\) in terms of \(y\) first.
Example: \(y = x\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 3\) gives a cone. \(V = \pi \int_{0}^{3} x^{2} \, dx = \pi \left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{3}\), which is \(\pi(9 - 0) = 9\pi\).
final.remember: Square the radius, multiply by \(\pi\), then integrate along the axis of rotation.

a.q: The curve \(y = \sqrt{x}\), from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 4\), is rotated about the x-axis. What is the volume of the solid?
a.why: \(V = \pi \int_{0}^{4} (\sqrt{x})^{2} \, dx = \pi \int_{0}^{4} x \, dx\), which is \(\pi \left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{4} = \pi \times 8 = 8\pi\). Writing \(\pi \int \sqrt{x} \, dx\) gives \(\frac{16\pi}{3}\), which is wrong because \(y\) was not squared first.
a.clue: Square \(y\) before you integrate, and \((\sqrt{x})^{2}\) is simple.

b.q: The region under \(y = 2x\) from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 2\) is rotated about the x-axis. What is the volume of the solid?
b.why: \(V = \pi \int_{1}^{2} (2x)^{2} \, dx = \pi \int_{1}^{2} 4x^{2} \, dx\), which is \(\pi \left[\frac{4x^{3}}{3}\right]_{1}^{2} = \pi\left(\frac{32}{3} - \frac{4}{3}\right) = \frac{28\pi}{3}\). Forgetting to square the 2 gives \(\frac{14\pi}{3}\), which is wrong because the radius is \(2x\), so the 2 is squared too.
b.clue: The radius is \(2x\), so square the whole of it, including the 2.
